newsitem.title: FINLAND: No Finnish rate cut seen till DEM/FIM breaks 2.95.
newsitem.headline: No Finnish rate cut seen till DEM/FIM breaks 2.95.

text.p: Finland's central bank looks unlikely to use the interest rate tool to curb appreciation in the markka against the mark, at least until DEM/FIM reaches 2.95, economists said on Tuesday.
In the meantime, they said the central bank is likely to be quite comfortable intervening in the market to sell markka and add to its foreign currency reserves.
"If the markka strengthens to 2.95 per mark a rate cut would be back on the agenda," Merita Bank chief analyst Jukka Lepomaki said. @

Another economist, requesting anonymity, estimated that the markka would have to appreciate around six to seven percent from the 3.04 central parity rate where it was linked to ERM to trigger a Bank of Finland key rate cut.
Finland linked the markka to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism last October.
"I think the exchange rate versus the German mark will be allowed to fluctuate, with interventions used to balance it," Sirpa Wallius, economist at Merita Bank, told journalists.
"And if that doesn't work, then maybe rates would have to be used." @

Economists noted that Finland's foreign currency reserves are relatively low -- falling last year by 12.5 billion markka on 1995. The Bank of Finland's latest balance sheet showed an 88 million markka rise to 36.5 billion in the week to January 8.
"As foreign currency reserves are low it is not a problem for the central bank to deter the strengthening of the markka," said Lepomaki.
Another point supporting a rise in foreign currency reserves is that it would help Finland pay about 12 billion markka in interest on some 175 billion markka in foreign currency loans, they said.
But not all analysts were comfortable with the prospect of sustained central bank intervention.

"When intervening in the currency markets this way, the Bank of Finland de facto guides Finnish monetary policies to a more expansionary setting," analyst Petteri Hirvonen wrote in Davy Protos Stockbrokers' weekly report.
"The central bank has been devaluing the currency and at the the same time this type of intervention has led short term market rates lower," Hirvonen argued.
Big overseas investment and clearing houses have driven the recent appreciation of the Nordic currencies, and domestic analysts said they might have miscalculated with Finland.
"The Bank of Finland cannot be pressured into cutting rates as fast as Norway," Lepomaki said, adding that the markka has not been as undervalued as the Norwegian crown.
They also pointed out Norway's trade surplus is roughly double Finland's and on key rates, Norway last week cut from a higher level.

European officials have stressed that no decision has yet been taken on how exactly currencies will be valued at the start of EMU's third phase in 1999. An average of past exchange rates could be used as well as ERM central parity.
Nonetheless, markets at least seem to have a psychological focus on the central parity rate.
"(If the markka firmed significantly), Finland would have a hard time explaining why the markka should be linked at 3.04 central rate to monetary union," Lepomaki said.
